Adult individuals of Aulonocranus dewindti achieve a maximum total length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], a size that positions this species among the medium-bodied cichlids endemic to the Lake Tanganyika basin. This ultimate length is attained after several years of sustained somatic growth, during which the fish progress through successive juvenile stages before reaching their asymptotic dimensions. Field surveys conducted across rocky littoral zones indicate that males tend to cluster near the upper end of this size range, whereas females are slightly smaller on average, a pattern common among many maternal mouthbrooding cichlids. The species exhibits a moderately elongated body form that facilitates navigation through the complex interstitial spaces of the rubble and pebble substrates it inhabits. Growth increments, estimated from scale annuli and length-frequency distributions, suggest that the majority of asymptotic size is achieved within the first three to four years of life, after which further elongation proceeds very slowly. Comparative data from congeneric Aulonocranus species are scarce, but the recorded dimensions for A. dewindti are consistent with those of other invertebrate-browsing cichlids occupying similar trophic niches along the lake's eastern shoreline.

The onset of reproductive capability in this species is marked by the attainment of a total length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the transition from the immature sub-adult phase to functional gonadal activity. Individuals below this size are rarely observed participating in spawning aggregations or engaging in the elaborate courtship displays that characterize the breeding season. At this maturational milestone, the body mass of a typical individual is approximately 4.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 4.9 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions parameterized from a large sample of preserved specimens collected across multiple localities. This pubertal mass represents a substantial increase from the minute size at which the fish emerges from the egg, reflecting the considerable energetic investment in somatic tissues required before reproductive allocation can commence. The length at which puberty occurs is roughly half the ultimate adult length, a ratio that aligns with general expectations for iteroparous teleosts that maintain a prolonged adult lifespan after maturity.

Newly hatched prolarvae of Aulonocranus dewindti emerge from demersal eggs at a wet weight of 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams], an extraordinarily diminutive mass that reflects the small size of the yolk-laden oocytes from which they develop. This birth mass, corresponding to a dry weight on the order of a few tenths of a milligram, places the species at the lower end of the range reported for lamprologine and other Tanganyikan cichlid lineages. The yolk-sac larva is entirely dependent on endogenous reserves during the first several days post-eclosion, and the duration of this lecithotrophic phase is strongly influenced by ambient thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the peak reproductive output of this cichlid reaches approximately 90 young per breeding cycle [N_R_i = approximately 90 young per breeding cycle], with the species completing one breeding cycle per year [F_R_i = one breeding cycle per year], based on comparisons with the closely related Lethrinops parvidens. This annual fecundity is modest relative to many open-water spawning cichlids but is consistent with the constraints of a mouthbrooding reproductive mode.

The maximum somatic mass documented for fully grown adults of Aulonocranus dewindti is 38.4 grams [Wwi = 38.4 grams], a value that represents the upper boundary of body size for this species under natural lake conditions. This asymptotic wet weight is attained concurrently with the achievement of the 14-centimeter total length (14 centimeters) [Li = 14 centimeters] and reflects the allometric relationship between linear dimensions and body volume characteristic of this taxon. Individuals approaching this mass are typically reproductively active adults that have completed several breeding seasons and exhibit the full development of secondary sexual characteristics, including elongated dorsal filament rays in males. The body mass trajectory from the pubertal stage to the ultimate adult size involves an approximate eightfold increase in tissue, a pattern that suggests a prolonged period of post-maturation growth during which surplus energy is partitioned between somatic maintenance and reproductive effort. Comparative data from sympatric cichlid genera indicate that the maximum mass of A. dewindti is moderate relative to larger piscivorous species but substantially greater than that of many small rock-dwelling algae scrapers.

Under the stable thermal regime of Lake Tanganyika, where water temperatures in the littoral zone consistently hover near 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for Aulonocranus dewindti is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years]. This longevity estimate, compiled from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determinations, places the species within the range of moderate-lived cichlids that delay senescence until after several reproductive cycles have been completed. The six-year lifespan implies that individuals enjoy a reproductive window of several years during which they can contribute multiple cohorts to the population. The relatively extended post-maturation period is likely an adaptation to the stable but resource-limited benthic environment, where competition for invertebrate prey among adult conspecifics imposes an upper bound on growth rate and, by extension, on the pace of life history. Field observations of senescent individuals reveal progressive deterioration of fin condition and reduced feeding efficiency, hallmarks of physiological aging that ultimately lead to natural mortality.

A notable trait of the life history of Aulonocranus dewindti is the relationship between the body size at which individuals become reproductively active and the asymptotic dimensions they eventually attain. Achieving a total length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters] at the onset of sexual maturity, the species invests the remaining majority of its somatic growth potential, up to the full adult length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], in continued post-pubertal expansion. This pattern, in which the pubertal length is roughly half of the ultimate adult length, is characteristic of many iteroparous cichlids and reflects an evolutionary strategy that balances early reproduction with sustained growth capacity. Under the stable thermal conditions of the lake, where temperatures in the shallow littoral remain around 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] provides an extended window for repeated spawning events. The wet weight at birth of 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams] represents an extremely low initial mass, which imposes a strong selective pressure for rapid early growth and efficient yolk utilization during the prolarval stage, both mediated by the prevailing thermal conditions.
